title: Kotlin for Android Interviews
description: Kotlin algorithms, concurrency, Compose, and production Android decisions in short interview challenges.

courses.title: Kotlin for Android Interviews
courses.description: Kotlin algorithms, concurrency, Compose, and production Android decisions in short interview challenges.

chapters.title: 1 · Kotlin semantics
chapters.summary: Reason about nullability, equality, generics, and closed state.

lessons.title: Nulls and value behavior
lessons.explanation: Trace the runtime meaning of compact Kotlin code.

exercises.prompt: A nullable API nickname should display Guest only when null. Which expression preserves an empty but valid nickname?
exercises.explanation: Elvis handles null only. The empty string is not null and remains visible; the other fallbacks change that contract.

exercises.prompt: Two separately allocated data-class values have equal properties. What is true?
exercises.code:
data class User(val id: Int)
val a = User(7); val b = User(7)
options: a == b is false; a === b is true
a == b is true; a === b is false
exercises.explanation: Data-class equals compares primary-constructor properties; referential equality still distinguishes allocations.

exercises.prompt: A data class owns a MutableList. What happens after copy() and a mutation through the copy?
exercises.code:
data class Cart(val items: MutableList<String>)
val a = Cart(mutableListOf("tea")); val b = a.copy()
b.items += "rice"
options: Both carts see rice because copy is shallow
exercises.explanation: copy reuses nested references. Prefer immutable nested values or an explicit deep copy when independent mutation matters.

exercises.prompt: A property can change between a null check and use. Which approach gives a stable non-null local?
exercises.explanation: Capturing the nullable property once removes the check/use gap. A forced assertion can still fail if the property changes.

exercises.prompt: Which overload is called? Assume no member function exists.
exercises.code:
open class Animal
class Dog: Animal()
fun Animal.label() = "animal"
fun Dog.label() = "dog"
val pet: Animal = Dog()
exercises.explanation: Extensions resolve from the declared receiver type at compile time, unlike virtual member dispatch.

exercises.prompt: An API ID is mandatory. Which expression fails immediately with a useful domain error if missing?
options: val key = id ?: throw IllegalArgumentException("id missing")
exercises.explanation: Elvis can throw at the boundary. orEmpty silently accepts invalid input and !! loses context.

exercises.prompt: A request ID must be logged only when present, including an empty string if the API permits it. Which code follows that rule?
exercises.explanation: The safe call executes for every non-null string, including empty; it avoids inventing a value or crashing.

exercises.prompt: Fill the null-safe length; zero is required only for a null title.
exercises.explanation: The safe call yields a nullable length; Elvis converts only null to zero.

lessons.title: Types and ownership
lessons.explanation: Choose types and branches that express the real contract.

exercises.prompt: A screen must represent loading, loaded, and failed states without contradictory flags. Which model is strongest?
options: A string status plus nullable error
A sealed interface with distinct data-bearing cases
A nullable result plus isLoading Boolean
exercises.explanation: A sealed hierarchy makes illegal combinations unrepresentable and supports exhaustive when branches.

exercises.prompt: Why cannot MutableList<Dog> be passed to a function accepting MutableList<Animal>?
options: The function could insert a Cat into the Dog list
Generic types are erased before compilation
exercises.explanation: MutableList is invariant because writes would violate the original element type.

exercises.prompt: A function only reads Animal values. Which parameter can accept List<Dog> safely?
exercises.explanation: Kotlin List is covariant in its element type, so a List<Dog> can be read as a List<Animal>.

exercises.prompt: A mutable object is used as a HashMap key and a property in hashCode changes. What is the likely symptom?
options: Lookup by the same object may fail until the original bucket is used
The map automatically rehashes the key
exercises.explanation: Hash maps choose a bucket from hashCode at insertion; changing it breaks the lookup invariant.

exercises.prompt: A new PaymentState subtype is added. Which implementation most helps the compiler reveal missing UI handling?
options: A string comparison against class names
An exhaustive when expression over a sealed hierarchy without else
A when with else returning Unknown
A chain of nullable if checks
exercises.explanation: Omitting else forces the compiler to flag an unhandled sealed case after the model grows.

exercises.prompt: A function returns List<Event> backed by an internal MutableList. What guarantee does the return type provide?
options: Callers cannot mutate through that List interface, but the owner can still change it
The underlying list is deeply immutable
exercises.explanation: Read-only interfaces restrict the caller API; they do not freeze aliases or nested objects.

exercises.prompt: You configure a new builder and must return the same builder. Which scope function expresses that intent?
exercises.explanation: apply uses this as receiver and returns the original object. let and run return the lambda result.

exercises.prompt: Complete a state branch that handles every known subtype without a fallback.
exercises.explanation: when is an expression; sealed subtypes make exhaustive handling checkable.

chapters.title: 2 · Algorithms and collections
chapters.summary: Choose efficient structures and prove edge cases.

lessons.title: Lookup and aggregation
lessons.explanation: Build linear-time answers with explicit collection semantics.

exercises.prompt: You need counts for 100,000 event types. What gives expected linear total time?
options: A MutableMap<String, Int> updated once per event
Count each type by rescanning the full list
Sort the list once per event
Use a List and contains for each event
exercises.explanation: Expected constant-time hash lookup makes one pass O(n), with O(k) space for distinct types.

exercises.prompt: Two records share an ID. What risk does associateBy { it.id } introduce?
options: It stores both records in a list
It preserves the earliest record always
The later record replaces the earlier value for that key
exercises.explanation: associateBy maps one value per key; detect duplicates or use groupBy when all records matter.

exercises.prompt: You need the first appearance of each ID in the original order. Which design works in O(n) expected time?
options: Use a nested loop and append every match
Put records into an unordered Map and take values
Track a HashSet of seen IDs while filtering the list
Call distinctBy after sorting by ID
exercises.explanation: A seen set supports expected constant-time membership while a single pass preserves input order.

exercises.prompt: A list of n transactions is sorted by timestamp and then scanned once. What is the asymptotic time?
exercises.explanation: Comparison sorting dominates the linear scan. The scan does not multiply the sorting cost.

exercises.prompt: Amounts are integer cents and may exceed Int range in aggregate. What should the accumulation type be?
options: Int because each amount fits Int
exercises.explanation: Convert each amount before adding to a Long; floating point is a poor representation for exact cents.

exercises.prompt: Which expression increments a frequency without losing a first occurrence?
exercises.explanation: The Elvis default handles the absent key and the assignment stores the incremented result.

exercises.prompt: CSV rows with malformed numeric amounts must be rejected and reported. Which conversion supports that flow?
options: toLongOrNull() followed by an explicit error branch
exercises.explanation: toLongOrNull exposes parsing failure as data so the caller can report the row rather than crash.

exercises.prompt: Fill the expected constant-time membership structure for duplicate IDs.
exercises.template:
val seen = mutable____1<String>()
for (id in ids) if (!seen.add(id)) report(id)
exercises.explanation: A mutable set returns false from add when the ID already exists.

lessons.title: Windows and ordered input
lessons.explanation: Track invariants while reducing search cost.

exercises.prompt: For positive numbers only, a sliding window sums to target. When can the left pointer advance safely?
options: Whenever the sum is below target
exercises.explanation: With nonnegative values, shrinking cannot increase the sum; negative inputs would break this monotonic reasoning.

exercises.prompt: Find two values whose sum is target in a sorted ascending array. What is the O(n) strategy?
options: Start at both ends; move left up for a small sum and right down for a large sum
Move both pointers inward on every step
Binary search every pair of indices
exercises.explanation: Sorted order tells which pointer can change the sum in the needed direction.

exercises.prompt: Why is the usual grow/shrink window invalid when array values may be negative?
options: Negative values cannot be stored in Kotlin lists
A HashMap is mandatory for every array
Removing a negative can increase the window sum
exercises.explanation: The monotonic sum assumption fails. Prefix sums with a map may fit a target-sum variant.

exercises.prompt: Count subarrays with sum k when values may be negative. Which invariant supports O(n) expected time?
options: Reset the sum whenever it becomes negative
Count prior prefix sums equal to currentPrefix minus k
Store only the largest element so far
exercises.explanation: Each matching earlier prefix marks a valid subarray ending at the current index; seed prefix zero with count one.

exercises.prompt: Build lower-bound search for the first value at least target.
exercises.hiddenTests: For [1,2,2,4], target 2 returns 1; target 3 returns 3; target 5 returns 4; empty array returns 0.

guided.explanation: The half-open interval [lo, hi) keeps every possible answer. A qualifying mid remains in the range; a smaller mid is excluded.

exercises.explanation: The half-open interval [lo, hi) keeps every possible answer. A qualifying mid remains in the range; a smaller mid is excluded.

exercises.prompt: Two sorted event lists must be merged in chronological order. Which complexity is attainable?
exercises.explanation: Comparing the current heads emits each event once; output storage is O(n + m).

exercises.prompt: Transactions share a timestamp and must retain input order. What property must the chosen sort provide?
exercises.explanation: A stable sort preserves relative order of values whose comparator reports equality.

exercises.prompt: Fill the initial prefix count needed to include subarrays beginning at index zero.
exercises.template:
val counts = mutableMapOf<Long, Int>(____1)
var prefix = 0L
exercises.explanation: The empty prefix occurs once before any element; it allows a full-prefix match.

chapters.title: 3 · Coroutines and Flow
chapters.summary: Control lifetime, cancellation, state, and event delivery.

lessons.title: Structured concurrency
lessons.explanation: Tie work to ownership and make failure propagation explicit.

exercises.prompt: A search request should stop when its ViewModel is cleared. Where should it be launched?
options: A new untracked CoroutineScope for every query
exercises.explanation: viewModelScope is canceled with the ViewModel, preventing old screens from retaining work.

exercises.prompt: A suspend function parses a large file and then updates UI state. Which boundary is appropriate?
options: Use Dispatchers.IO for every CPU-bound operation
Run parsing with withContext(Dispatchers.Default), then update UI in the caller context
exercises.explanation: Default is intended for CPU work. withContext returns to the parent context and preserves cancellation.

exercises.prompt: A broad catch(Exception) wraps a suspending request. What must happen to cancellation?
options: Ignore cancellation because it is an Exception
Rethrow CancellationException rather than convert it to a recoverable error
exercises.explanation: Swallowing cancellation allows work to continue after its owner ends.

exercises.prompt: Two child async operations run in a normal coroutineScope. One fails. What happens by default?
options: The scope converts failure to null
The scope cancels siblings and propagates the failure
The other child always succeeds independently
exercises.explanation: Regular structured concurrency treats an uncaught child failure as a scope failure; supervisorScope changes that policy.

exercises.prompt: Independent dashboard tiles should continue if one fetch fails. Which structure fits?
options: supervisorScope with each child handling its own error
exercises.explanation: Supervision isolates child failures while keeping the whole operation bounded by its parent.

exercises.prompt: User searches A then B; A responds last. Which design avoids showing A results?
options: Use a longer timeout for A
Put both results into one mutable list
Cancel or identify the old request and accept only the latest query result
exercises.explanation: Response order is not request order. Cancellation or a generation check protects the current query.

exercises.prompt: What is the issue with runBlocking inside an Android click handler?
options: It dispatches work to Main automatically
It blocks the main thread and can freeze UI
It always creates a memory leak
exercises.explanation: runBlocking waits synchronously. Launch owned coroutine work instead of freezing the event loop.

exercises.prompt: Fill the dispatcher for CPU-bound image analysis in a suspending function.
exercises.explanation: Default is designed for CPU-bound work; Main would monopolize UI rendering.

lessons.title: Flow and shared state
lessons.explanation: Choose streams with the right replay and lifecycle behavior.

exercises.prompt: A screen needs the current connection state immediately after subscription. Which stream fits?
options: A cold Flow that never emits initially
exercises.explanation: StateFlow always holds a latest value, which new collectors receive.

exercises.prompt: A one-off toast event should not replay after screen recreation. Which default is closest?
exercises.explanation: An event stream with no replay avoids delivering a stale toast to a new collector; delivery while absent still needs a product decision.

exercises.prompt: A Fragment collects UI Flow. What prevents collecting while its view is stopped?
options: repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED) in the view lifecycle scope
exercises.explanation: repeatOnLifecycle starts and cancels collection with the view lifecycle, avoiding invisible UI work.

exercises.prompt: Each query should cancel the previous search stream when a new query arrives. Which operator fits?
exercises.explanation: flatMapLatest switches to the newest inner Flow and cancels the previous collection.

exercises.prompt: A typeahead should avoid requests for intermediate keystrokes and duplicate terms. Which pipeline fits?
options: debounce then distinctUntilChanged before request mapping
exercises.explanation: Debounce waits for quiet input; distinctUntilChanged avoids identical consecutive terms before network work.

exercises.prompt: A repository Flow emits cached rows and then network sync fails. Which error policy preserves offline content?
options: Keep the cached rows and expose sync failure separately
Delete the cache to show an empty state
Treat the failed network result as an empty authoritative list
exercises.explanation: A sync failure does not invalidate previously committed local data. Keep source-of-truth state separate from refresh status.

exercises.prompt: Two coroutines increment MutableStateFlow<Int>. Which update avoids lost increments?
options: Read value once and write later
Use a Boolean flag without synchronization
exercises.explanation: update applies an atomic compare-and-set loop; read-modify-write on value can lose an increment.

exercises.prompt: Fill the operator that cancels a previous search when a new query arrives.
exercises.explanation: flatMapLatest switches the active inner stream to the most recent query.

chapters.title: 4 · Android and Compose
chapters.summary: Model UI state, recomposition, lifecycle, and navigation.

lessons.title: Compose state and identity
lessons.explanation: Make state ownership and list identity explicit.

exercises.prompt: A text draft should survive activity recreation. Which local state holder fits?
options: A new value inside every recomposition
exercises.explanation: rememberSaveable persists supported values through recreation; remember only survives recomposition.

exercises.prompt: A parent owns selected filter and two children must agree on it. Where should state live?
options: In the parent, passed down as value and change callback
exercises.explanation: Hoisting gives one source of truth and makes both children reflect the same selection.

exercises.prompt: A reorderable LazyColumn keeps row-local expanded state. What avoids state appearing on the wrong row?
options: Recreate the list on every frame
Use stable item keys derived from item IDs
exercises.explanation: Stable keys bind remembered row state to the item identity rather than its current position.

exercises.prompt: An expensive filtered list depends only on query and source list. What avoids recalculating on unrelated recompositions?
options: Always call filter in a LaunchedEffect with no keys
A mutable global cache with no invalidation
Run filter in every draw modifier
exercises.explanation: A keyed remember recalculates when inputs change, while avoiding unrelated work. Measure before adding caching.

exercises.prompt: A composable starts a request on every recomposition. Which fix makes the effect follow itemId?
options: Launch in the composable body again
Use remember with no keys to start a coroutine
Block composition until the request finishes
exercises.explanation: LaunchedEffect scopes the task to composition and restarts it only when its key changes.

exercises.prompt: A mutable list is changed in place but UI does not update. Which model makes changes observable?
options: Keep mutating the same plain ArrayList
Move the list to a companion object
Expose immutable UI state and replace the list in a StateFlow update
exercises.explanation: Compose observes state reads; replacing immutable snapshots makes changes explicit and testable.

exercises.prompt: A screen has loading, content, and recoverable error. What is the main benefit of modeling these as a sealed type?
options: It removes the need for tests
It prevents showing content and loading as contradictory independent flags
It forces every screen to be a singleton
exercises.explanation: Distinct states make rendering and transition tests easier to reason about.

exercises.prompt: Fill the state holder that survives a configuration recreation for a saveable string.
exercises.explanation: rememberSaveable saves supported values beyond recomposition through activity recreation.

lessons.title: Lifecycle and navigation
lessons.explanation: Choose owners and back stack behavior deliberately.

exercises.prompt: An activity rotates during a repository fetch. Which owner normally retains screen state across recreation?
exercises.explanation: ViewModel outlives configuration recreation and exposes state to the new UI owner.

exercises.prompt: A details screen needs an article. What should navigation pass?
options: A stable article ID, then load through the repository
exercises.explanation: IDs are small, serializable route inputs; the destination can restore data after process death.

exercises.prompt: The process dies while a screen is open. Which data must be recoverable from durable storage rather than ViewModel memory?
options: Committed user progress and queued edits
exercises.explanation: ViewModels do not survive process death. Durable progress requires persistence.

exercises.prompt: A singleton repository stores an Activity reference. What is the risk?
options: The Activity can remain reachable after destruction
exercises.explanation: Long-lived objects retaining short-lived Contexts can leak screens; use application context where appropriate.

exercises.prompt: A repository is shared by several ViewModels. Which ownership best fits?
options: Pass an Activity instance as global state
Application-level dependency graph with repository abstraction
Construct a new repository in every recomposition
Store it in a composable local variable
exercises.explanation: A long-lived injected repository has a clear owner and can be replaced by a fake in tests.

exercises.prompt: Bottom tabs recreate the same destination on each tap. What navigation option commonly avoids duplicate top copies?
options: launchSingleTop with appropriate state restore behavior
Add every tap as a new destination
Clear the whole database on tab change
exercises.explanation: Single-top navigation avoids stacking identical destinations; save/restore state handles tab switching.

exercises.prompt: A feature needs location permission. When is a request most understandable?
options: Only after a location API throws
When the user begins the location feature, with context for why
exercises.explanation: Contextual permission requests align the system prompt with a user action and support a denied state.

exercises.prompt: Fill the ViewModel scope for a request tied to this screen state.
exercises.explanation: viewModelScope is canceled when the ViewModel is cleared; lifecycleScope belongs to a lifecycle owner.

chapters.title: 5 · Production Android scenarios
chapters.summary: Keep local data authoritative and recover safely from failure.

lessons.title: Offline data and jobs
lessons.explanation: Connect persistence, networking, and work scheduling.

exercises.prompt: A feed must display cached items offline and refresh when online. Which layer should the UI observe?
options: A Room Flow; network writes verified updates into Room
An in-memory list cleared at launch
A network call before every row draw
exercises.explanation: A local source of truth gives immediate offline state; sync changes it transactionally.

exercises.prompt: An order and its line items must commit together. What prevents a half-written order?
options: A Room transaction around related writes
exercises.explanation: A database transaction either commits the related records or rolls them back together.

exercises.prompt: A small upload should retry after process death when network returns. Which Android tool fits?
options: WorkManager with network constraints and retry policy
exercises.explanation: WorkManager persists deferrable work across process death and can enforce connectivity constraints.

exercises.prompt: A server reply arrives after a newer local edit. What prevents the reply from overwriting the edit?
options: Compare versions or timestamps and apply a defined conflict rule
Always trust the last arriving response
Clear local state before the reply
exercises.explanation: Arrival order is not causal order. Versioned records let sync decide whether an update is stale.

exercises.prompt: A 500 response and a malformed 200 response need different diagnostics. Which handling is best?
options: Separate transport/status failures from decoding failures
Treat all failures as empty success
exercises.explanation: Distinct errors help recovery and debugging; a malformed successful payload is not the same as server failure.

exercises.prompt: An upload can be retried after a timeout that may have occurred after server commit. What makes retry safe?
options: Generate a new ID on every retry
Send a stable operation ID understood by the server
exercises.explanation: An idempotency key allows the server to recognize repeated delivery of one logical operation.

exercises.prompt: A schema change adds a required column to saved records. What must a release provide?
options: A migration or a deliberate documented destructive policy
Only a new Kotlin data class
exercises.explanation: Existing databases need a migration path; changing the entity alone does not transform stored rows.

exercises.prompt: Fill the storage primitive for a durable offline queue that survives process death.
exercises.explanation: A Room insert persists the pending edit; UI state alone cannot survive process death.

lessons.title: Reliability and payments
lessons.explanation: Reason through retries, callbacks, and state machines.

exercises.prompt: Thousands of clients receive 503 simultaneously. Which retry policy avoids synchronized spikes?
options: Retry only from a UI recomposition
Exponential backoff with jitter and a retry cap
Immediate retry in a tight loop
Exactly one fixed one-second retry forever
exercises.explanation: Jitter spreads load; caps avoid unbounded resource use. Only retry operations safe to repeat.

exercises.prompt: A payment request times out. Which local state is truthful before reconciliation?
exercises.explanation: A timeout does not prove whether the server committed. Query by stable operation ID before retrying.

exercises.prompt: Bluetooth connect callbacks arrive after the user disconnects. What guards the state machine?
options: Apply every callback in arrival order
A connection generation token checked before applying callbacks
exercises.explanation: A generation or session ID rejects stale callbacks from prior connection attempts.

exercises.prompt: A webhook-like event may be delivered twice. What prevents two balance updates?
options: Assume the network never duplicates events
Transactionally record the event ID and apply the effect once
exercises.explanation: Deduplication must be durable and atomic with the effect; an in-memory check races and resets.

exercises.prompt: A production crash occurs while parsing payment records. What is the safer diagnostic?
options: Include the entire request body in analytics
Log a correlation ID and sanitized error category
Log full card and token values
exercises.explanation: A correlation ID lets engineers trace failures without leaking sensitive fields.

exercises.prompt: Two refreshes finish out of order. What keeps local data at the newest version?
options: Compare authoritative revision before committing each response
Use only the UI spinner state
exercises.explanation: Persisting a revision check ensures a late old response cannot replace newer data.

exercises.prompt: Fill the operation identifier used unchanged across payment retries.
exercises.explanation: A stable idempotency key identifies one logical charge across network retries.

exercises.prompt: Build a safe offline payment command
exercises.story: A checkout queues one charge while offline. A worker may restart and requests may time out. Complete each stage of the local command flow.

parts.prompt: Persist a command before attempting delivery.
parts.hiddenTests: Queue one order; assert one pending row with a stable order ID and one scheduled job.

guided.explanation: Use the stable order ID, persist the pending charge, then enqueue delivery.

parts.expected: Use the stable order ID, persist the pending charge, then enqueue delivery.

parts.prompt: Retry without issuing a second logical charge.
parts.hiddenTests: After a timeout, retry with the same command ID; a confirmed response marks the row complete exactly once.

guided.explanation: Send the original ID as the idempotency key, mark confirmed commands complete, and retry uncertain outcomes later.
